'''''Echinochimaera''''' ("prickly chimaera") is an [[extinct]] [[genus]] of [[Chimaera|chimaeriform]] [[fish]], known from the Lower Carboniferous [[Bear Gulch Limestone]] in [[Montana]], [[United States]]. It is one of the earliest Chimaeriformes known.

[[File:Echinochimaera meltoni pair.png|thumb|Life restorations of a pair of ''Echinochimaera meltoni'' including a female (top left) and a male (bottom right)]]

== Taxonomy ==
The genus' name derives from the [[Greek language|Greek]] ''εχινό'' (''echino'') meaning spiny, and [[chimaera]]. It is assigned to the [[Order (biology)|order]] [[Chimaeriformes]].<ref name="paleobio-db" /> 

=== Species ===
The two known ''Echinochimaera'' species lived in the [[Upper Mississippian]] ([[Serpukhovian]]).<ref name="UMPC-5374">{{cite web|url=http://www.cas.umt.edu/paleontology/search/details.cfm?catalogno=5371&refer=browse|title=University of Montana Paleontology Center|date=2007-11-01|accessdate=2009-09-26|archive-date=2010-06-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100628000215/http://www.cas.umt.edu/paleontology/search/details.cfm?catalogno=5371&refer=browse|url-status=dead}}</ref> Fossils of the species were found in the [[Bear Gulch Limestone]] in [[Montana]], [[United States]].

Both species have rounded bodies and paddle-like tails as well as large [[Pectoral fin|pectoral]] fins, two [[dorsal fin]]s and a [[jaw]] fused to the [[braincase]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://school.discoveryeducation.com/schooladventures/prehistoricsharks/gallery2.html|title=Search for Ancient Sharks|publisher=Discovery Education|accessdate=2009-10-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091210093705/http://school.discoveryeducation.com/schooladventures/prehistoricsharks/gallery2.html|archive-date=2009-12-10|url-status=dead}}</ref> The paddle-like tails indicate that ''E. meltoni'' was likely not a predator nor a fast swimmer.<ref name="lund-1990">{{cite journal|last=Lund|first=Richard|year=1990|title= Chondrichthyan life history styles as revealed by the 320 million years old Mississippian of Montana |journal=Environmental Biology of Fishes|publisher=Springer Netherlands|volume=27|issue=1|pages=1–19|issn=1573-5133|doi=10.1007/BF00004900}}</ref><ref name="bear-gulch-meltoni">{{cite web|url=http://www.sju.edu/research/bear_gulch/pages_fish_species/Echinochimaera_meltoni.php|title=Fossil Fishes of Bear Gulch - Echinochimaera meltoni|date=2006-02-01|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120212145647/http://www.sju.edu/research/bear_gulch/pages_fish_species/Echinochimaera_meltoni.php|archivedate=2012-02-12|accessdate=2015-12-09}}</ref>

==== ''Echinochimaera meltoni'' ====
[[File:†Echinochimaera meltoni Lund 1977 (cropped).jpg|left|thumb|Specimen of ''E. meltoni'']]
''E. meltoni'' was first described by Richard Lund, an [[Adelphi University]] [[palaeontologist]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sju.edu/research/bear_gulch/pages_other/other_lund.php|title=Bear Gulch - About Richard Lund|date=2006-11-16|accessdate=2009-09-27|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100108080608/http://www.sju.edu/research/bear_gulch/pages_other/other_lund.php|archivedate=2010-01-08}}</ref> in 1977.<ref name="paleobio-db"/><ref name="UMPC-5374"/> The fossils found of ''E. meltoni'' have shown a great deal of [[sexual dimorphism]], with males being found to have a maximum body length of {{convert|15|cm|in|abbr=on}}  while that found in females was only {{convert|7|cm|in|abbr=on}}. Juveniles were {{convert|1.3|-|2|cm|in|abbr=on}} long. In general, the females only grew to about half the size of the males.<ref name="lund-1990"/> Males also had four pairs of spikes which may have been used to defend against [[predator]]s and to identify the fish as male.<ref name="bear-gulch-meltoni"/>

There was a relative abundance of immature male fossils found, and that together with the significant sexual dimorphism indicate there was extreme [[sexual selection]] among the species.<ref name="lund-1990"/>

==== ''Echinochimaera snyderi'' ====
''E. snyderi'' was described, like ''E. meltoni'', by Richard Lund. It was described in 1988 based on juvenile specimens, all with a body length under {{convert|9|cm|in|abbr=on}}. ''E. snyderi'' differs from ''E. meltoni'' in fin detail as well as jaw shape and teeth near the front edge of the face rather than a tooth plate. Mature specimens discovered later suggest this species' adult size to be larger than ''E. meltoni''.<ref name="bear-gulch-snyderi">{{cite web|url=http://www.sju.edu/research/bear_gulch/pages_fish_species/Echinochimaera_snyderi.php|title=Fossil Fishes of Bear Gulch - Echinochimaera snyderi|accessdate=2009-09-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100729173527/http://www.sju.edu/research/bear_gulch/pages_fish_species/Echinochimaera_snyderi.php|archive-date=2010-07-29|url-status=dead}}</ref>
